claims.text: Vault is not open source; it uses the Business Source License model.
Pulumi ESC is fully open source and Apache 2.0 licensed, whereas HashiCorp Vault uses Business Source License 1.1.
Vault stores secrets only, whereas Pulumi ESC stores environments, secrets, and configurations.
Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments so shared configuration is inherited.
Pulumi ESC environments can reference secrets stored in Vault, and those secrets can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
Pulumi ESC can store non-secret configuration alongside secrets kept in Vault.
Pulumi ESC is a fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud; Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting requires significant management overhead.
Pulumi ESC supports pulling secrets from multiple sources including HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, and AWS Secrets Manager; Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault.
Pulumi ESC supports both a GUI and a Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking; Vault's editor is limited and offers a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle.
Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI and supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
The `vault` CLI reads and writes secrets but does not inject them as environment variables.
Vault Agent's process supervisor mode can inject secrets as environment variables (covers that use case separately).

The Pulumi Service Provider allows management (create, update, delete) of ESC collections of secrets and configuration as a resource; Vault individual secrets can be managed with the Vault provider for Pulumi or Terraform.
Vault has no equivalent concept to environment composability; secrets are organized by path convention and structure is maintained by hand.
Vault secrets are individually versioned.
Pulumi ESC values can be secret or plaintext, whereas Vault values can only be secrets.
Pulumi ESC lets users see existing secrets, whereas Vault does not.

In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment and updates propagate automatically to downstream environments; Vault has no first-class environment to reference so secrets are read by path.
Pulumi ESC supports string interpolation to construct dynamic values; Vault does not support interpolating values from other values.
Pulumi ESC environments can be forked for testing/branching; Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
`pulumi env diff` shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment; Vault has no equivalent.
Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions such as toJSON, fromJSON, fromBase64, and toString.
Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
Vault's security barrier encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
Pulumi ESC uses OIDC flows to generate dynamic credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
Vault cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, and each engine is configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint them.
Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and pulumi-service provider.
Configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
